newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Chellgren to take Ashland helm.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Chellgren to take Ashland helm.

text.p: Ashland Inc President Paul Chellgren said he expects to stay the course at Ashland Inc after becoming the fourth chief executive officer in the 72-year old company's history next week.

That strategy includes a decision made several years ago to steer growth capital away from the diversified oil refining and marketing company's refining operations, said Chellgren, who is set to become chief executive on October 1 and slated to add the title of chairman in January 1997.

Refining capital expenditures will be held to the level of depreciation as part of the company's plans to invest 75 percent of its capital in its chemicals, construction, Valvoline lubricants and other non-refining businesses by 2000, up from about 65 percent in 1995.
"I think there's going to be a lot of continuity and consistency in that (strategy)," Chellgren said.

Ashland has a modest production-sharing pact in Nigeria, where it produces about 20,000 barrels of oil per day, but nearly all the oil fed into its 355,000 barrel per day U.S. refineries is acquired under contract or on the spot market.

Chellgren said Ashland -- an active buyer of crude this year from the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve -- can obtain all the oil it needs in the highly efficient world oil markets. "Having your own crude supply as a pure refiner-marketer in some ways is perhaps a little bit less important today as it was ten or fifteen years ago," he said.
In recent years, Ashland has obtained about 100,000 barrels per day (bpd) under Middle Eastern contract, 100,000 bpd from Canada and 120,000 bpd from domestic and foreign spot purchases, he said.
"These markets are increasingly transparent and perfect and you can get the volumes, you just have to pay the price," he said.

As Chellgren takes the helm, Ashland will be paying that price in the short run. Tensions in the Middle East fueled a run-up in crude prices that was expected to trim earnings for the fourth quarter ending September 30, he said.

But as those tensions fade and oil prices move lower, Ashland sees long-term advantages for its three U.S. refineries, which are located in the Midwest. Additional pipeline capacity into the Midwest, particularly Mobil Corp's decision in particular to reverse a crude pipeline from Chicago to Ohio, will increase the flow of Canadian crude.

"When they did that, we could get Canadian crude to our two southern refineries -- Canton (Ohio) and Cattletsburg (Ky.) -- and that's been important to us. In essence that Canadian crude has meant we are buying less offshore crude," he said.
